text: Ernst Karl Abbe HonFRMS (23 January 1840 – 14 January 1905) was a German businessman, optical engineer, physicist, and social reformer. Together with Otto Schott and Carl Zeiss, he developed numerous optical instruments and was a co-owner of Carl Zeiss AG, a German manufacturer of scientific microscopes, astronomical telescopes, planetariums, and other advanced optical systems. Born on 23 January 1840 in Eisenach, Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, to Georg Adam Abbe and Elisabeth Christina Barchfeldt, Abbe came from a humble background—his father was a foreman in a spinnery—and was supported by his father's employer to attend secondary school at the Eisenach Gymnasium, where he graduated in 1857 with strong academic performance and evident scientific talent. Despite financial difficulties, his father funded his studies at the Universities of Jena (1857–1859) and Göttingen (1859–1861), during which Abbe gave private lessons to supplement his income. He earned his PhD from Göttingen on 23 March 1861. Influenced by Bernhard Riemann and Wilhelm Eduard Weber, both members of the Göttingen Seven, he completed short assignments at the Göttingen observatory and the Physikalischer Verein in Frankfurt, founded by Johann Wolfgang von Goethe in 1824 and still active today. On 8 August 1863, he qualified as a university lecturer at the University of Jena; in 1870, he became an associate professor of experimental physics, mechanics, and mathematics in Jena; and attained full professor status by 1879. He became director of the Jena astronomical and meteorological observatory in 1878. In 1889, he joined the Bavarian Academy of Sciences and Humanities and the Saxon Academy of Sciences. He was relieved of his teaching duties at the University of Jena in 1891. Abbe died on 14 January 1905 in Jena and was an atheist. In 1866, he became a research director at the Zeiss Optical Works and in 1868 invented the apochromatic lens, which eliminates both primary and secondary color distortion. By 1870, he invented the Abbe condenser for microscope illumination. In 1871, he designed the first refractometer, described in a booklet published in 1874. By 1872, he developed the laws of image formation for non-luminous objects. Zeiss Optical Works began selling his improved microscopes in 1872, including models with homogeneous immersion objectives by 1877 and apochromatic objective microscopes by 1886. He created the Abbe number, a measure of a transparent material's variation of refractive index with wavelength, and Abbe's criterion, which tests for a systematic trend in observations and specifies that angular separation cannot be less than the ratio of wavelength to aperture diameter in terms of resolving power. Already a professor in Jena, he was hired by Carl Zeiss to improve the manufacturing process of optical instruments, which was initially based on trial and error. Abbe was the first to define the numerical aperture as the sine of the half angle multiplied by the refractive index of the medium between the cover glass and front lens. He is credited with discovering the resolution limit of the microscope and the formula (published in 1873), although Helmholtz noted in a 1874 publication that Joseph Louis Lagrange had derived it earlier, six decades prior. Helmholtz offered Abbe a professorship at the University of Berlin, which he declined due to his ties with Zeiss. Abbe supported the wide aperturists, arguing that microscopic resolution is ultimately limited by the aperture of the optics, though he also acknowledged that other parameters should be considered in objective design. In his 1874 paper "A Contribution to the Theory of the Microscope and the Nature of Microscopic Vision," Abbe stated that resolution is inversely dependent on aperture without proposing a formula for the resolution limit. In 1876, he was offered a partnership by Zeiss and began sharing in the profits. Although earlier theoretical derivations of the resolution formula existed, Abbe was the first to reach the conclusion experimentally. In 1878, he built the first homogeneous immersion system for microscopes. The objectives developed through the Abbe-Zeiss collaboration achieved ideal ray geometry, allowing Abbe to determine that aperture sets the upper limit of microscopic resolution, not lens curvature or placement. Abbe first published the resolution formula in 1882, stating that both theoretical and experimental investigations confirmed it. His contemporary, Henry Edward Fripp, placed Abbe and Helmholtz's contributions on equal footing and perfected the interference method by Fizeau in 1884. In 1884, Abbe, Zeiss, Roderich Zeiss (Zeiss's son), and Otto Schott formed the Jenaer Glaswerk Schott & Genossen, which developed and produced 44 initial types of optical glass and eventually merged with Zeiss Optical Works. Working with telescopes, he built an image reversal system in 1895. To produce high-quality objectives, Abbe made significant contributions to diagnosing and correcting optical aberrations, including spherical and coma aberrations, necessary to achieve the resolution limit defined by the formula. He also discovered that rays in optical systems must have constant angular magnification over their angular distribution to produce a diffraction-limited spot, known as the Abbe sine condition. His work was so advanced that Frits Zernike based his phase contrast research on it, earning him the Nobel Prize in 1953, and Hans Busch used it in developing the electron microscope. During his time with Carl Zeiss, Abbe advanced optics and promoted labor reform. He founded the social democratic Jenaische Zeitung in 1890 and introduced the eight-hour workday in 1900, in memory of his father's 14-hour workday. He also established a pension fund and a discharge compensation fund. In 1889, he founded and endowed the Carl Zeiss Foundation for scientific research with the aim of securing the economic, scientific, and technological future and improving employee job security. He emphasized that employee success should depend solely on ability and performance, not origin, religion, or political views. In 1896, he reorganized the Zeiss optical works into a cooperative with profit-sharing. His social policies were so influential that they were adopted as a model by the Prussian state and idealized in Alfred Weber's 1947 book Schriften der Heidelberger Aktionsgruppe zur Demokratie und Zum Freien Sozialismus. A crater on the Moon named Abbe honors him. Abbe was a pioneer in optics, lens design, and microscopy and a leading authority of his time, leaving behind numerous publications on his findings, inventions, and discoveries.
